implementation_notes: The BCL carries both halves. Immutable list/dictionary/set types are immutable and, per the namespace Remarks, give 'implicit thread safety in multi-threaded applications (no locks required to access collections)' while sharing structure between versions, so a writer's copy is not a deep copy of every element. Publication has its own helper: ImmutableInterlocked.Update 'mutates a value in-place with optimistic locking transaction semantics via a specified transformation function ... retried as many times as necessary to win the optimistic locking race', and the class also offers InterlockedExchange/InterlockedCompareExchange for ImmutableArray. That replaces a hand-written counted body: the GC owns the reference count and the snapshot reference is what gets published atomically. A counted handle of your own remains justified only around unmanaged memory, where the count must outlive the collector's view.
pitfalls: Immutable collections are a read-path optimisation: every mutation allocates a new version (and ImmutableList<T> updates are O(log n) with real constants), so a hot write path turns into allocation and GC pressure - ConcurrentDictionary/ConcurrentBag are the right shape for write-heavy maps.

Immutable is a property of the collection, not of what it stores: elements remain ordinary references, so mutating a stored object is still visible to every reader of the snapshot - store immutable values or copies.

The optimistic Update loop can run your transformation several times: the lambda must be pure and side-effect-free (a counter increment inside it fires once per retry), and the snapshot must be read once into a local rather than through several property reads.
